How to Calculate EMI for a Car Loan in Nepal (With Examples)

18 November 2025 · 4 min read · Finance

Buying a car in Nepal is, for most people, a financing decision first and a purchase decision second. With new car prices running into tens of lakhs and banks typically financing 70–80% of the invoice value, the number that actually decides affordability is not the sticker price — it is the monthly EMI.

This guide shows you exactly how EMI is calculated, walks through a complete worked example with realistic Nepali figures, and points out the inputs that move the number the most. At the end, you can run your own figures through the free Loan Calculator.

What EMI actually is

EMI stands for Equated Monthly Installment — the fixed amount you pay the bank every month until the loan is fully repaid. Every installment contains two parts:

  1. Interest on the outstanding balance (large at the start), and
  2. Principal repayment (small at the start, growing every month).

Because the interest portion shrinks as you pay down the balance, the same monthly amount slowly shifts from "mostly interest" to "mostly principal" — this is called amortization.

The formula

The standard amortization formula for a fixed-rate loan is:

EMI = P × r × (1 + r)ⁿ ÷ ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1)

Where:

  • P is the principal (the amount you actually borrow, not the car price),
  • r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), and
  • n is the number of monthly installments (years × 12).

The most common mistake is plugging in the annual rate directly. The formula needs the monthly rate — for an 11% loan that is 0.11 ÷ 12 = 0.009167.

A worked example with Nepali numbers

Suppose you are buying a car invoiced at Rs. 42,00,000. The bank agrees to finance 80%, so your down payment is Rs. 8,40,000 and the loan amount is:

P = Rs. 33,60,000

Assume an 11% annual rate (typical for auto loans from commercial banks in Nepal in recent years) and a 5-year tenure:

  • r = 11 ÷ 12 ÷ 100 = 0.009167
  • n = 5 × 12 = 60 months
  • (1 + r)ⁿ ≈ 1.7289

EMI = 33,60,000 × 0.009167 × 1.7289 ÷ (1.7289 − 1) ≈ Rs. 73,050

So the bank takes roughly Rs. 73,050 every month for 60 months. The total you repay is 73,050 × 60 = Rs. 43,83,000, which means the interest cost of the loan is about Rs. 10,23,000 — nearly a third of the car's price.

Worth knowing

In lakh-style grouping (the en-IN locale used across this site for Nepal and India), the monthly figure reads Rs. 73,050 and the interest reads Rs. 10,23,000 — always double-check which grouping a figure uses before comparing offers.

The five inputs that move your EMI

  • Loan amount, not car price. A bigger down payment shrinks P and cuts interest for the entire tenure, not just the first year.
  • Interest rate. On this example, moving from 11% to 12.5% pushes the EMI to roughly Rs. 75,600 — over Rs. 1.5 lakh more interest across the life of the loan. Always compare the effective rate including processing fees.
  • Tenure. Stretching 5 years to 7 years lowers the EMI but raises total interest sharply, because interest compounds over more months.
  • Fixed vs. floating rate. Many Nepali auto loans are floating, repriced against the bank's base rate. Ask how often the rate reviews and what your EMI would be at base rate + 3%.
  • Fees. Processing fees (often ~1%), insurance requirements and prepayment penalties change the effective cost even when they do not change the EMI.

How to use the calculator

Open the Loan Calculator, enter the amount you plan to borrow (car price minus your down payment), your bank's annual rate, and the tenure in years. It returns the monthly payment, total interest and total repayment instantly — so you can compare a 5-year and a 7-year offer, or two banks' rates, in seconds.

The takeaway

The EMI formula is simple; the discipline is in comparing total interest, not just the monthly figure. Two offers with nearly identical EMIs can differ by lakhs over the life of the loan. Run both through the calculator, look at the interest total, and let that decide.
